newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus electoral chief evicted, crisis brewing.
newsitem.headline: Belarus electoral chief evicted, crisis brewing.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko's security forces barred Belarus's top electoral official from his office on Friday and Western diplomats said the former Soviet republic's political crisis was deepening.
Parliamentarians, trying to stop Lukashenko seizing more power in a referendum set for November 24, appealed to world leaders for help against what they called approaching dictatorship.

"We ask the international community...to offer political and moral support to parliament and a people which has survived many tragedies this century," parliamentary leader Semyon Sharetsky told a news conference, reading from a statement.
Earlier, scuffles broke out when Lukashenko's personal security guards prevented Viktor Gonchar, head of the Central Commmission on Elections and Referendums, from entering his office.

Gonchar, who had been appointed by parliament and who was sacked by Lukashenko on Thursday, had vowed not to recognise the referendum in which Lukashenko is seeking to boost his powers significantly in defiance of the constitution.
Lukashenko, 42, meanwhile was addressing thousands of people called to a pre-referendum rally in the eastern industrial city of Mogilyov, where he got a lukewarm welcome.
Deputies called an emergency session and agreed impeachment proceedings should begin against Lukashenko -- though he has ignored rulings by rival institutions in the past.

Political analysts have been comparing the crisis in Belarus to a legal stalemate in Moscow in December 1993 which President Boris Yeltsin put down with tanks. The tense mood in Minsk grew significantly darker on Friday.

Sharetsky told Reuters deputies might occupy the chamber. "An extreme situation could develop where a quick decision will have to be taken. I do not exclude the possibility that the president will break up parliament," he said.
Parliamentary leaders called Western diplomats to a special gathering to discuss the crisis at which Sharetsky passed on the appeal for help.

"The political crisis in Belarus has radically worsened. Of course the West will react on the appeal. But President Lukashenko has shown several times that he doesn't care about the West's opinion," one diplomat said.

Another diplomat described the reaction to Gonchar's sacking. "For the first time ever I saw people go silent and look frightened. The next question is, who's next? They all expected this, but what's worrying is it's happening so fast".

Opponents of Lukashenko, whose rule has grown increasingly authoritarian since he won a landslide victory on a platform of rebuilding a union with Moscow and fighting corruption in July 1994, say they fear he is building a dictatorship.
"Today in Belarus power is being seized and an open dictatorship is being set up under the guise of a referendum," Sharetsky said of the poll.
The statement, signed by all senior parliamentarians, also urged Russian President Boris Yeltsin to call an extraordinary summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States.
The Human Rights Watch-Helsinki monitoring group expressed concern at events in Belarus in a statement which said the referendum, if Lukashenko won, would be a "death knell for democracy".

Lukashenko would win the right to extend his term by more than two years without elections, appoint half the constitutional court and half the electoral commission, and create an upper house of parliament partly appointed by him.
